title: Confidence Elicitation: A New Attack Vector for Large Language Models

contributions.purpose: Show that confidence elicitation - asking a closed-source LLM for its own uncertainty - can serve as a new attack guidance signal in a fully black-box (hard-label) setting where only the final prediction is normally available.
contributions.mechanism: Introduce confidence elicitation attacks (CEAttack): query the model to elicit calibrated confidence, approximating soft-label probabilities via a Dirichlet-mean estimate; first empirically verify the elicited confidence is calibrated and not hallucinated for current LLMs.
contributions.evaluation: Empirically show elicited confidence is calibrated and not hallucinated on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct across SST-2, AG-News, StrategyQA; establishes confidence as usable attack feedback (first to point out confidence elicitation may be at odds with robustness).
contributions.domain: LLM adversarial robustness / security (text classification attacks)
contributions.source_quote: Novel Attack Vector: We are the first to investigate whether confidence elicitation can be used as a potential attack vector on LLMs, while providing strong motivations for why anyone would want to take this approach.

contributions.purpose: Generate adversarial examples by using elicited confidence as feedback in black-box optimization, even when the model's confidence is imperfectly calibrated.
contributions.mechanism: Bottom-up word-substitution attack: progressively substitute up to |W|=5 words with counter-fitted-embedding synonyms, retaining substitutions that lower the elicited class confidence in a hill-climbing greedy loop, bounded by a semantic-quality constraint epsilon.
contributions.evaluation: Across three datasets and two models, black-box optimization succeeds even with imperfectly calibrated models; metrics include Accuracy Under Attack, ASR, semantic similarity (USE), perplexity, query counts, attack time.
contributions.source_quote: Effective Black-Box Optimization: We demonstrate that confidence elicitation can be used effectively as feedback in black-box optimization to generate adversarial examples. Our evaluation across three datasets and two models illustrates that black-box optimization is achievable even with imperfectly calibrated models.

contributions.purpose: Achieve state-of-the-art hard-label black-box word-substitution attacks on LLMs, improving over prior hard-label methods that require many queries.
contributions.mechanism: CEAttack's more direct bottom-up optimization path (vs. top-down over-perturb-then-repair of SSPAttack) finds high-risk regions closest to the original input, cutting queries and time.
contributions.evaluation: Compared to SOTA hard-label technique SSPAttack (also TextHoaxer, Self-Fool Word Sub), CEAttack achieves better Attack Success Rate with fewer queries and higher semantic similarity on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct over SST-2, AG-News, StrategyQA.
contributions.source_quote: State-of-the-Art Hard-Label Attack on LLMs: Our methodology achieves state-of-the-art performance in hard-label, black-box, word-substitution-based attacks on LLMs. Compared to the current state-of-the-art hard-label optimization technique (SSPAttack), our method results in better Attack Success Rates (ASR) with fewer queries and higher semantic similarity.

self_declared_provenance.quote: In this paper, we demonstrate that it is possible to approximate soft labels, essentially allowing for a hard-label attack with more information. This is achieved through the technique of confidence elicitation (Xiong et al., 2024), where we simply ask the model for its own uncertainty.

Left) SSPAttack and other previous hard-label attacks first (A) perform multiple word substitutions, so that a heavily perturbed sample is misclassified ... Right) In contrast, CEAttacks take a bottom-up approach (positions the method against SSPAttack, Liu et al., 2023).

we obtain a set S of synonyms sourced from Counter-fitted embeddings (Mrksic et al., 2016) ... We compare our guided word substitution attacks, CEAttack to 'Self-Fool Word Sub' from (Xu et al., 2024), TextHoaxer (Ye et al., 2022) and SSPAttack from (Liu et al., 2023).

notes: Accept. Predominantly positive SOTA claims (better ASR, fewer queries, higher semantic similarity than SSPAttack). Key caveat: the method assumes a classification setting and depends on the model's elicited confidence being reasonably calibrated - authors note it works 'even with imperfectly calibrated models' but calibration is a load-bearing assumption. Scope is limited to word-substitution attacks on two 7-8B open models and three classification datasets; generative-task and jailbreak extensions are left as future work. No explicit negative/tie result reported in abstract/intro; results framed as consistently favorable.
